blocks.text: The chapter unfolds in two movements. Verses 1-8 announce a renewed creation in which the former order, death, grief, and pain pass away. Verses 9-27 enlarge the vision by portraying New Jerusalem as both the Lamb's bride and a radiant city. The closing emphasis is not merely on magnificent buildings: God and the Lamb are the city's temple, and God's glory is its light.

The language of a new heaven and new earth belongs to a scriptural movement extending from creation to new creation. Along that movement, creation is declared good, human vocation is given, the world becomes disordered, and the Creator remains the object of wisdom and worship. The chapter's language of a restored city and divine dwelling also stands within the history of exile and return: Assyrian and Babylonian exile, Persian-period return, the rebuilding of city and temple, and the continuing hope for complete restoration.

Revelation uses apocalyptic imagery, a way of portraying divine rule and the fate of earthly powers through vivid symbols such as cosmic changes, beasts, and significant numbers. Such writing arose among communities facing pressure, exile, or persecution and asking how God would act. This helps explain why the city's enormous measurements, precious materials, repeated twelves, and absence of night should be read as a coordinated vision rather than as ordinary civic description.

The promise that death will be no more was striking in settings where death was commonly treated as final. Resurrection hope affirms God's power over death and the renewal of his people, although bodily resurrection was debated within Second Temple Judaism. Against that background, the removal of death, mourning, crying, and pain describes a far-reaching reversal, not simply an improvement in present circumstances.

sections.title: Why Jerusalem Is the Named City

blocks.text: Jerusalem had gathered associations with Davidic rule, temple presence, pilgrimage, repentance, judgment, and hoped-for restoration. It had also stood under imperial pressure and remained central to priestly authority and messianic hope. Calling the descending city “New Jerusalem” therefore brings together royal, communal, and worship-related associations, while the vision transforms them around God's direct presence.

sections.title: From Tabernacle to a City without a Temple

blocks.text: The statement that the city has no temple comes after a long sequence of sacred-space imagery: divine presence in the wilderness tabernacle, Solomon's temple in Jerusalem, the temple's judgment and destruction, restored Second Temple worship, and Jesus' identification with temple fulfillment. Revelation 21 reaches the sequence's stated conclusion: New Jerusalem needs no separate temple because God and the Lamb dwell there as its temple.

sections.title: The Nations and the Open Gates

blocks.text: The vision includes more than the city's internal beauty. Nations walk by its light, kings bring their glory into it, and its gates remain open because there is no night. At the same time, nothing unclean or false may enter. The imagery therefore places the nations' honor within a city defined by God's light and holiness, while entry remains limited to those written in the Lamb's book of life.

Biblical sanctuary passages share the language of dwelling and holiness, but the tabernacle, First Temple, Second Temple, Christological metaphor, community metaphor, heavenly sanctuary, and new creation are not interchangeable referents. Revelation's declaration that God and the Lamb are the temple should therefore be read in its own new-creation setting. Later Christian interpretations of this imagery cannot legitimately support antisemitism, replacement claims, seizure or destruction of holy places, or immunity from ethical accountability.

sections.title: The Vision within Revelation's Larger Scriptural Pattern

blocks.text: Across Revelation and into the following chapter, New Jerusalem combines the imagery of city, bride, sanctuary, Eden, and renewed Zion. Revelation repeatedly reworks Israel's Scriptures, especially imagery associated with Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. Its reuse of Ezekiel includes throne, scroll, measuring, battle, city, river, and tree imagery arranged within Revelation's own literary sequence.

sections.title: The Significance of God's Direct Presence

blocks.text: A temple ordinarily gathered together holy space, sacrifice, priesthood, purity, mediation, pilgrimage, and the divine presence. That background makes the absence of a temple in New Jerusalem especially significant: the passage does not describe a city without God's presence, but one in which the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are themselves its temple. The city's defining reality is therefore direct divine presence rather than access centered on a separate sanctuary.
